articles.title: Why I changed my smart TV DNS settings (and how to do it)
articles.author: Jayric Maning
articles.content:
Nothing frustrates me more than stuttering, broken playback on my smart TV. I tried a few other fixes to solve my smart TV buffering problems, but after changing my smart TV DNS settings, I'm living in a buffering and stutter-free world.
Changing DNS improved my TV streaming
A small tweak with a big payoff
I've experienced the frustration of waiting for shows to buffer or apps to load. What I didn't realize was that a quick DNS change could solve many of these annoyances. DNS (Domain Name System) is a protocol that translates website names into the IP addresses needed to access your streaming services. When your smart TV wants to access Netflix, it needs to convert "netflix.com" into an actual server address — and that process happens through a DNS server.
Most of us use whatever DNS server our internet provider assigns by default, but these ISP-provided DNS servers are often not optimized for performance. It creates a hidden bottleneck that affects your streaming experience, even if you have a high-speed internet subscription.
After researching alternatives, I decided to test Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 DNS service. Cloudflare operates a massive global network with servers in over 300 cities worldwide. This extensive infrastructure means DNS queries can be resolved much faster than traditional ISP servers.
After using DNSperf to test Netflix connections, my default DNS settings produced an average response time of 88 milliseconds. After switching to Cloudflare's DNS, that number lowered to just 28 milliseconds, which is a huge improvement! This translates to noticeably faster loading times for streaming apps and less frustrating buffering during peak usage hours, making it an effective way to eliminate buffering on my smart TV.
Beyond speed improvements, Cloudflare's public DNS also includes extra security benefits. The service automatically helps protect against phishing attacks and malware-infected websites. It also provides privacy protection compared to many ISP DNS services, which sometimes log and sell browsing data.
How I changed DNS on my smart TV
It only takes a few minutes
Changing the DNS settings on your smart TV might sound technical, but it's actually pretty simple once you know where to look.
- Grab your remote and press the Settings button. Head over to the Network settings panel and select your current Wi-Fi network (or Ethernet if you're wired in).
- Now, look for the IP settings. By default, this is usually set to Automatic or DHCP, but you'll want to switch it over to Static. You'll need to provide a specific IP address that your smart TV will use on your network.
- In DNS server fields, enter 1.1.1.1 as your primary DNS (that's Cloudflare's fast, privacy-focused server).
- Once you've filled in those numbers, save your changes and restart your TV. That's it! You've now switched your smart TV to use faster, more reliable DNS servers.
See if the streaming apps tend to load faster and videos start playing with less delay. If you ever want to go back, just switch the settings from Static back to Automatic.
Keep in mind, the exact menu names might vary a little depending on your smart TV, but the steps will be around the same. If you get stuck, your TV's manual or support site can help you find the right menu. Furthermore, while using a static IP address is handy, it can also create issues if you reset your router.
Using Cloudflare as your primary DNS can potentially give you speed, security, and reliability — all with just a few quick changes in your settings. Give it a try and see how your streaming experience improves.
Should you change your TV's DNS settings?
Here's when it's worth it
Should you change your TV's DNS settings? If you stream a lot and want smoother, faster performance, it's definitely worth considering. Switching to a public DNS service like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 can make apps load quicker and videos start almost instantly.
Public DNS providers such as Cloudflare and Google offer more reliable connections because their networks rarely slow down, even during busy hours. There's also a security advantage: services like Cloudflare automatically block many phishing and malware sites, adding extra protection while you browse and stream.
If you're interested in accessing content from other regions, some smart DNS services can also help you unlock shows and movies unavailable in your country. This perk is especially appealing if you want to explore a wider range of streaming libraries.
While changing DNS settings might sound like advanced tech tinkering, it's actually one of the simplest yet most effective tweaks you can make to improve your Smart TV's performance without spending a dime on hardware upgrades or faster internet plans.
However, while most modern TVs and apps handle custom DNS settings well, a few might not work perfectly, and some ISPs may even try to force your connection back to their own DNS servers, which could cause potential issues. It's also important to remember that using a public DNS means trusting a new company with your browsing data, so it's wise to review their privacy policy — Cloudflare, for example, is known for its strong privacy stance.
Overall, the benefits of changing your DNS, including faster streaming, greater reliability, and enhanced security, often outweigh the minor drawbacks. The process takes just a few minutes, and you can always switch back if you don't notice an improvement. I recommend at least giving it a try.
articles.summary:
Updating your smart TV's DNS settings to a third-party provider like Cloudflare can significantly reduce buffering and improve streaming speeds by bypassing slower, default internet service provider servers.

### Key Points
- Changing DNS settings from automatic to static allows users to manually input faster, more reliable servers like Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1.
- Testing shows that switching to Cloudflare can reduce DNS response times from 88 milliseconds to 28 milliseconds.
- Public DNS services often provide enhanced security features, such as automatic protection against phishing and malware-infected websites.
- The configuration process involves accessing the network settings menu on a smart TV and updating the DNS server fields manually.
- Users can revert to default settings at any time by switching the network configuration back to automatic or DHCP mode.

### Why it Matters
Optimizing DNS settings is a cost-effective way to enhance home entertainment performance without requiring expensive hardware upgrades or higher-tier internet plans. This simple technical adjustment can resolve persistent streaming bottlenecks and provide users with a more secure, private browsing experience.

articles.title: Lexar's SL500 Might Become Part of Your Everyday Kit
articles.author: Kim Simpson
articles.content:
Phone-based content creation has moved well past quick behind-the-scenes clips. Photographers are now shooting more polished promo videos with their phones on a regular basis. That workflow shift changes what your phone needs to be capable of, and internal storage and speed are usually the first barriers. A high-quality portable SSD is worth investing in to help your phone keep up with demands.
Have you ever had the need to quickly delete videos on your phone to free up space after your recording was interrupted by a “storage full” notification? No one wants to see that pop up when you are in the middle of recording something important. With a growing need to film, edit, and post content filmed on smartphones, file management is important in keeping devices running at full capability.
The Storage Problem
With technological advances increasing with each major smartphone release, data consumption is growing. A single 48 MP ProRAW photo is approximately 75 MB, and capturing 4K 30 fps footage in Apple ProRes 422 HQ generates a data footprint of approximately 6.6 GB per minute. When BTS content and more polished promo work are being shot on smartphones, that data adds up fast. Running out of space mid-shoot isn't an option when there's a deadline attached, and constantly deleting or offloading to the cloud is a distraction that no one needs.
This is where the need for SSD storage arises, and a device that is made for your smartphone will help to organize your workflow seamlessly. Lexar’s SL500 Portable SSD provides fast, portable storage that isn't tied to one device. Shoot on the phone, offload to the drive, keep shooting. Move the same files to an iPad or MacBook for a quick edit without redownloading anything from the cloud. It sounds simple because it is, but simple is exactly what you want when you're working against the clock.
Speed That Supports Video
The SL500 is rated for up to 2,000 MB/s read and 1,800 MB/s write speeds over USB 3.2 Gen 2x2. That's fast enough to shoot ProRes video directly to the drive rather than to internal storage, and fast enough that transferring a day's footage doesn't become a coffee-break-length wait. For anyone producing 4K promo content alongside quick social clips, that speed is paramount in keeping the flow of your workday going. Recording ProRes directly to an external drive is supported on iPhone 15 Pro models and later Pro models, and the SL500 supports this over USB-C.
Key Tech Specs
- Interface: USB 3.2 Gen 2x2.
- Read speed: Up to 2,000 MB/s.
- Write speed: Up to 1,800 MB/s.
- Enclosure: Slim aluminum unibody.
- Thickness: As thin as 4.8 mm.
- Durability: IP54 dust and water resistance.
- Shockproof: Drop-resistant up to 6.6 feet (2 meters).
- Encryption: Lexar DataShield software with 256-bit AES encryption.
Keeping Work and Personal Separate
Shooting client and BTS content on a personal phone can leave everything tangled together, with a collection of work-based content sitting in between family snaps and pictures of your Sunday brunch. Using a dedicated drive for work content keeps all of that separate, with everything work-related living in one organized place.
Built to Travel
At as little as 4.8 mm thick, with a slim aluminum unibody construction, this is a drive that is compact enough not to burden your kit bag. The Mag Set version includes a magnetized protective sleeve that allows the drive to attach securely to a compatible phone, which means you can still work one-handed on location rather than fumbling with a handheld drive while holding your smartphone in your other hand.
Capacity and Compatibility
The SL500 comes in 1 TB, 2 TB, and 4 TB capacities. For most day-to-day work, 1 TB gives enough headroom for organizing and shooting clips from your shoot day without needing to manage space carefully. If you, for example, are shooting as a wedding content creator, you might want to invest in a higher capacity to ensure no interruptions to your day. The SL500 works across PC, Mac, Android devices, and iPhone 15 series or later, so it isn't tied to one ecosystem, which is great news when switching between a work phone and a personal one, or between your own kit and a colleague's.
Final Thoughts
Lexar’s SL500 Portable SSD is compact, fast, and built for ease of use over a day's shooting. As phone-shot content moves from quick BTS clips to more polished promo work, the gap between what phone storage offers and what that work demands keeps widening. External storage fast enough to record directly is no longer optional for a growing number of creators, and investing in a quality product from a trusted brand is vital for keeping your work safe and secure.

### Key Points

articles.title: Usage Intelligence: The Monetization Signal Most AI Companies Are Ignoring
articles.author: Pierluigi Paganini
articles.content:
The AI Paradox
There is a paradox: AI companies exist to extract intelligence from data, yet many have almost no visibility into how their own software is being used.
They design complex models, introduce their product, set a price, and then hope that customers renew their contracts. In a space as fast-paced as AI, such a strategy is no longer safe.
Without usage as a guide, price decisions are made on assumptions rather than facts. Product roadmaps are driven by story, not by usage. Customer success teams learn about customer churn when renewal dates are approaching.
In reality, usage intelligence has become one of the most important signals in an AI business, guiding everything from pricing strategy to product development and long-term monetization.
Why AI Changes the Stakes for Usage Data
AI changes the economics of software and, with it, the relevance of usage visibility. The economics of existing software products are linear in cost, whereas those of AI products are not. Compute, energy consumption, as well as third-party model licenses, can all be material variable costs.
If usage increases rapidly (through enterprise adoption, agents, or workflows), the cost can grow faster than the revenue generated if pricing is not aligned with consumption.
The opposite scenario is just as dangerous. If customers are not using key capabilities, churn may be approaching long before a renewal conversation begins.
Research shows the extent of this visibility gap. For AI vendors, visibility is important on the commercial side, too. They need to know how customers are using the AI capabilities they sell. IDC research found that 48% of software buyers want better visibility into their usage.
The pace of change is also a concern, with 70% ranking rapid change in the AI ecosystem among their top three AI-related security risks. Pricing, packaging, and business models must evolve at the same pace, and that requires reliable usage intelligence.
What Usage Intelligence Actually Looks Like
Of all the capabilities that make up a software monetization strategy, usage intelligence is the one most commonly treated as optional — and the one that most consistently separates companies that adapt from those that don’t. It is the feedback loop that connects real-world product consumption back to the decisions that shape pricing, packaging, and product direction.
At the instrumentation layer, usage intelligence starts with telemetry data. This includes activation events, entitlements consumed, feature-level data, daily and monthly active users, and time-to-value metrics that track how quickly customers get value from the product. Thales Sentinel can also collect usage data from on-premises, offline, and disconnected environments, so vendors are not limited to tracking always-connected software.
The operational layer is where all the telemetry data is made actionable. Usage dashboards in CRM systems enable account teams to see how customers use the software. Health scores can even detect reduced engagement well before any risk of renewal is seen.
The enforcement layer makes sure that usage is consistent with contract rights. This is particularly important for consumption-based or token-based pricing schemes. Tracking accuracy is essential for determining customer fairness and vendor revenue.
Finally, there is the feedback loop. The insights from usage need to flow back to those responsible for pricing, packaging, product development, and customer success. Without the feedback loop, the data is just more information.
Pricing specialists have long argued for incremental experimentation. Research from Simon-Kucher reveals that companies that make frequent, data-informed pricing adjustments tend to achieve stronger growth than those that depend on static pricing models.
Usage intelligence provides the evidence required to make those adjustments with confidence.
How Usage Data Enables Multiple Business Models
Business model agility is increasingly becoming a competitive advantage for AI companies, yet flexible business models cannot exist without trustworthy usage data beneath them.
Consumption-based pricing, outcome-based pricing, token models, and hybrid subscription structures all depend on accurate measurement of how customers use the product. There is demand for these models, too. IDC research found that 45% of software buyers prefer usage-based models.
In practice, most AI companies adopt a gradual sequence.
They begin with subscription licensing to establish predictable recurring revenue. As adoption grows, they instrument feature usage and engagement patterns. That data then enables the introduction of consumption or token-based layers tied to high-value AI capabilities.
One AI audio-recognition company did just that. It moved from perpetual licensing to several subscription tiers using Thales Sentinel. Its usage data showed which features customers used most, which helped the company decide how to structure those tiers without making changes to the core technology.
Another AI recognition vendor delivering SDKs for embedded systems took a different approach using Sentinel. Their trial licenses expire after a defined number of executions instead of after a fixed time period. This usage-based trial model demonstrates genuine customer interest, giving them a clearer indicator of product-market fit than a simple time-limited evaluation would.
Both examples show that usage intelligence transforms monetization strategies from guesswork into evidence-based decision-making.
From Data to Decision: Three Practical Applications
The real value of usage intelligence lies in informing concrete business decisions.
Preventing churn is one of the most immediate uses. Feature-level engagement metrics can detect declining usage several months before a renewal date. This enables customer success teams to step in and show the value or introduce underutilized features, preventing a customer from leaving.
Upsell and expansion opportunities can also show up in the usage data. Seat utilization may show that a team is close to capacity and needs more licenses. Feature usage can show when a customer is getting enough value from certain capabilities to justify moving to a higher tier or adding consumption-based features.
Usage data can also inform the product roadmap. Rather than relying on assumptions about what customers want, AI companies can see which features people use and which get little attention. This is key in a market full of similar AI capabilities. Companies need to know which parts of their product customers value and are willing to pay for.
There is also a need for the collection of usage intelligence to be privacy-conscious. For vendors operating under frameworks such as GDPR or the EU’s AI Act, it is necessary to design telemetry systems that prioritize aggregated data collection over personal data collection whenever possible.
The Organizational Challenge
However, technology alone is not enough to create usage intelligence. Businesses must also ensure that the intelligence is available to those who can act on it.
Usage intelligence only delivers value if it reaches the people who can act on it. Pricing teams need consumption data to make confident adjustments to their models. Product teams need feature engagement data to inform roadmap decisions rather than rely on assumptions. Sales teams need account-level signals to time their conversations correctly. Customer success teams need early warning indicators to intervene before disengagement becomes churn. Finance teams need usage trends to build credible revenue forecasts.
Getting that data to all of those functions consistently and in a usable form requires intentional data architecture and a shared organizational commitment to treating monetization as a cross-functional capability rather than a single team’s responsibility.
This becomes harder as companies add more AI products. If usage data is split across separate products, teams may struggle to see how a customer is using the wider portfolio. Bringing the data together can show where products are being heavily used, where adoption is low, and where there may be room to expand an account.
Building Systems Around Innovation
The AI companies that sustain long-term commercial success are the ones who built a system around it that can learn, adapt, and improve as markets shift and customer needs evolve.
Usage intelligence is what makes that system adaptive. Without it, pricing decisions are made on assumptions, packaging tiers are defined by intuition, and churn arrives without warning. With it, every commercial decision — what to charge, how to package, what to build next, which customers need attention — is grounded in evidence rather than expectation.
In an industry defined by rapid innovation, the AI companies that listen to their own usage data will be the ones best positioned to turn experimentation into sustainable growth.

### Key Points

- IDC research indicates that 48% of software buyers demand better visibility into their usage, while 70% view rapid ecosystem changes as a top security risk.

articles.title: A Botnet Used Poetry To Mine Crypto From Over 3,000 Servers - Here's How
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Briley Kenney)
articles.content:
A Botnet Used Poetry To Mine Crypto From Over 3,000 Servers - Here's How
You can file this next bit of news under a creative but uniquely sophisticated category of software engineering. Black Lotus Labs security researchers have discovered a new botnet, powering a rather insidious malware campaign, called PoeLLM. Like any other malware, the goal is to infect as many systems as possible and take control — this one scoops up infected machines into a botnet to build a remote web of servers. What's different about it, however, is that it utilizes a poem, published on GitHub, to issue and deploy commands. Once infected, the compromised machines use a command-and-control (C2) process to phone home to a server, and the location or key to that server is issued through the poetry.
When the actor in control of the malware changes the words in the poem on GitHub, the infected machines use them to derive the new C2 server address. As for how the botnet and the infected systems are being used, it was mostly to mine and steal cryptocurrency and glean insight from other sensitive data sources.
Per Luman Technologies report, Black Lotus Labs first picked up network communications from a compromised system in June 2026, when it phoned home. The peak of the malware attack occurred later that month, eventually involving nearly 2,200 infected servers, with up to 800 active daily. So far, 3,400 servers have been infected, with the common denominator involving systems running vulnerable versions of open-source LLM and AI tools, such as Ollama and LiteLLM. Additional servers were vulnerable and compromised via Gotenberg, an open-source PDF converter.
How did the poem actually work?
Machines infected with the malware look up the poem, extract the address, and connect to a remote server for further instructions, becoming AI-powered proxies. Mainly, the instructions were used to infect more machines or mine cryptocurrency. The poem, "On the Nature of Connection," likely AI-generated itself, was disguised inside a nondescript file and hosted on a GitHub repository. Four fixed words peppered into the text served as the key for a remote IPv4 address. Also hardcoded into the malware was a crude cipher, a dictionary that matched words to corresponding numbers. Together they directed infected machines to a C2 server address.
In one example, the cipher mapped words to numbers as follows: driver to 92, diode to 119, decryption to 164, string to 74. Infected machines converted the words to the numbers, then used those to build the complete C2 server address: 92 dot 119 dot 165 dot 74. The hacker only had to swap out those words for others to change the address, sending compromised systems to a different C2 command server. The poem has been updated at least 11 times since its discovery. Alongside crypto miners, the malware employed a suite of additional tools that empowered infected clients to find and exploit new systems. That's a classic recipe for building a botnet, like the recent Russian example that was linked to more than 10 million devices before it was shut down.
This automated setup allows hackers to focus on multiple vulnerabilities across services, paving the way for a much larger pool of compromised systems. It's also an example of how AI solutions are becoming a huge cybersecurity concern, drastically accelerating both attacks on networks and their defenses. It's mostly supercharging and speeding up attacks, finding vulnerabilities quickly, as we've seen with PoeLLM.
What's next and what's happening with the PoeLLM botnet?
Per Lumen Black Lotus, three of the twelve C2 IP addresses discovered by the team are still active. The team also lists additional infrastructure IPs that may still be compromised and part of the campaign.
The Lumen article points out that open-source LLM tools like LiteLLM, Ollama, and Gotenberg need more secure APIs, especially with AI tools constantly probing for new attack vectors. Researchers claim open-source LLMs are distinctly vulnerable because they're often hosted on decentralized local or cloud infrastructure that isn't as secure as more locked-down traditional on-premises servers. In addition, open-source tools use external libraries or dependencies, which can be vulnerable, much like the compromised PoeLLM repository. Most of the affected systems were also running software with outdated patch sets, highlighting another important point: keep your tools up to date.
PoeLLM primarily targeted and affected enterprise and commercial servers, but it's still a good lesson for everyone that attackers are using more sophisticated tools and becoming more creative with their approaches every day. Everyone else mounting a defense should have strong monitoring in place to help identify potential vulnerabilities and compromised machines. Lumen Black Lotus recommends consistent network log inspections, with special attention on anomalous behavior, and adherence to network best practices. That includes regular hardware reboots and installing all software updates in a timely manner. At home, something as simple as rebooting your router can help flush potential malware and compromised packages. It's also risky to skip major firmware updates; you could be looking at a compromised network, and that exposes any devices connected to it. Staying on top of modem, router, and device updates is a must.
articles.summary:
Security researchers at Black Lotus Labs have identified a sophisticated botnet called PoeLLM that uses AI-generated poetry on GitHub to hide command-and-control instructions for cryptocurrency mining.

### Key Points
- The PoeLLM botnet has compromised over 3,400 servers, peaking at 800 active daily infections in June 2026.
- Malware uses a poem titled "On the Nature of Connection" to derive remote server addresses via a hardcoded word-to-number cipher.
- Primary targets include enterprise servers running vulnerable versions of open-source AI tools like Ollama, LiteLLM, and the PDF converter Gotenberg.
- Attackers update the poem on GitHub to dynamically redirect infected machines to new command-and-control infrastructure.
- Lumen Technologies reports that three of the twelve identified command-and-control IP addresses remain active.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights the growing security risks associated with decentralized, open-source AI infrastructure that often lacks robust API protections. It demonstrates how attackers are increasingly using creative, automated methods to bypass traditional detection and maintain persistent control over enterprise networks.

articles.title: Elon Musk wants to take on Verizon and AT&T. The price tag could be staggering.
articles.author: Jake Conley
articles.content:
'It's not something that gets done overnight': SpaceX's telecom ambitions will be hard-won, CEOs and analysts say
Elon Musk wants SpaceX (SPCX) to take on America's largest cell service providers, but matching the telecom giants' vast wireless networks could take years and billions of dollars, executives and analysts warned this week.
SpaceX, which already operates the world's largest commercial satellite network with Starlink, is in talks with major telecommunications infrastructure companies to secure access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States, Bloomberg reported. The move would advance Musk's ambitions to establish a fourth nationwide wireless carrier alongside the three traditional telecom and mobile service incumbents: Verizon (VZ), AT&T (T), and T-Mobile (TMUS).
The announcement sent stock in AT&T and T-Mobile falling by as much as 6% on Friday, while Verizon declined by a thinner 1.5%.
Satellite launches through Starlink and spectrum acquisitions "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call.
But breaking into an industry whose dominant players have spent decades building out infrastructure, acquiring spectrum, and cultivating millions of subscribers will be no easy feat.
"It's not something that gets done overnight," AT&T CEO John Stankey told analysts on his company's earnings call Wednesday, before the latest details of SpaceX's plans emerged. "It takes a lot of years and a huge level of investment to get to the kind of performance levels that customers have become accustomed to in scaled networks."
SpaceX's tower negotiations, which reportedly include cell tower operator Crown Castle (CCI), represent one of the clearest indications yet of the scale of SpaceX's ambitions. They also illustrate the substantial financial and technological barriers facing Musk as he attempts to challenge America's entrenched telecommunications giants.
The company's reported target of 80,000 cell sites would put its planned network on a scale comparable to that of the three incumbents. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile each lease space on approximately 60,000 to 80,000 US cell towers combined, according to Goldman Sachs analysts, while the country has roughly 175,000 traditional cell towers nationwide, per data from SNL Kagan.
The cost for such a build-out would be immense, even for a company with the capitalization and balance sheet of SpaceX. The average cellular tenant pays roughly $50,000 per year to lease space on a cell tower, according to Goldman Sachs analysts led by Michael Ng. At that rate, an 80,000-tower network could generate approximately $4 billion in annual rental payments, or between $20 billion and $40 billion over a typical five- to 10-year leasing period.
articles.summary:
SpaceX is pursuing an ambitious plan to challenge major U.S. wireless carriers by negotiating access to 80,000 cell sites to establish a nationwide Starlink mobile network.

### Key Points
- SpaceX is in talks with infrastructure firms like Crown Castle to secure space on 80,000 cell towers across the United States.
- The initiative aims to position Starlink as a fourth major wireless carrier alongside incumbents Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile.
- Goldman Sachs analysts estimate that leasing 80,000 cell sites could cost SpaceX approximately $4 billion annually in rental payments.
- Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile fell by up to 6% following reports of the company's aggressive expansion strategy.
- Industry experts warn that matching the performance and infrastructure scale of established telecom giants will require years of significant capital investment.

### Why it Matters
This expansion represents a significant competitive threat to the established telecommunications oligopoly that has dominated the U.S. market for decades. If successful, SpaceX could fundamentally alter the wireless landscape by leveraging its satellite network to provide nationwide mobile coverage.

articles.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
articles.author: Terrence O’Brien
articles.content:
It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn’t all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro.
What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
Apple’s long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, an OLED iPad Mini, and more.
Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro
A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.
This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.
It’s also going to stick with the M5 series of chips for the time being — specifically, the M5 Pro and M5 Max. There might not be an M6 Pro or Max, even. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year.
M6 MacBook Pro
That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. It might also get a slight redesign, including a hole-punch style camera. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.
M6 iMac
The iMac is also expected to get an M6 update, nearly two years after its last revision. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model.
OLED iPad Mini
Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. articles.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Blessing or a Curse?
articles.author: James Mapes
articles.content:
“Generative AI is one of the most exciting and powerful technologies of our time,
but it also presents new challenges and
risks that we need to address thoughtfully and proactively.”
-Sam Altman
Is every great invention a blessing or a curse?
What if one of humanity’s greatest inventions became its biggest threat?
Can something that gives us so much freedom also take it away?
Can technology meant to bring people together actually push them apart?
The truth is that every major technological breakthrough comes with hope. The internal combustion engine promised freedom. Social media promised connection. Now, artificial intelligence promises something even bigger: the chance to expand human intelligence.
History shows us a clear lesson: every big invention has a downside. Cars gave us mobility but also pollution. Social media connected billions, but many people feel more alone than ever. Now, AI is here, offering what once seemed like science fiction. The real question isn’t just what AI can do, but what we decide to do with it.
Here’s the big question: Are we getting smarter because of technology, or are we slowly giving up our ability to think for ourselves?
Take the internal combustion engine. It changed society, gave us more mobility, created wealth, and reshaped daily life. But it also caused pollution, made us rely on fossil fuels, and led to millions of road deaths.
Then social media arrived. Suddenly, we could talk to people anywhere, share ideas right away, and give almost anyone a public voice. But this amazing invention also brought new ways to manipulate, isolate, and mislead people, and created new kinds of addiction.
Now, artificial intelligence is here. It might be the biggest leap forward we’ve ever seen.
My question is: Will AI help us imagine more, or will it replace our imagination? Will it make us more creative or just more dependent? Will it help us understand ourselves better, or just tell us what we want to hear?
The answer depends more on our intentions, imagination, and sense of responsibility than on the technology itself. Does technology make us better, or does it create problems we never saw coming?
Both the internal combustion engine and social media changed the world. They created huge opportunities but also led to results their inventors probably never imagined.
The internal combustion engine.
Here are three negatives:
- Environmental damage. Burning gasoline and diesel releases greenhouse gases and air pollutants, causing climate change, respiratory illness, and environmental degradation.
- Deaths and injuries. Car accidents have become a major cause of preventable death and injury. Technology meant to give us more freedom and also brought serious risks.
- Dependence on fossil fuels. Our world now relies on petroleum, which has led to global conflicts, economic risks, and communities built around highways and cars.
Three positives:
- Freedom and mobility. The automobile gave ordinary people unprecedented independence. People could travel farther, choose where to live, pursue employment opportunities, and explore beyond their immediate communities.
- Economic growth and job creation. The combustion engine helped transform transportation, agriculture, manufacturing, and commerce. It created millions of jobs.
- Greater productivity and access. Tractors revolutionized farming, trucks accelerated the delivery of goods, and motorized emergency vehicles improved access to medical care and disaster response.
The invention of social media:
Here are three negatives:
- Mental health and social comparison. Social media can encourage unhealthy comparisons, anxiety, cyberbullying, and addictive patterns of use. Ironically, a technology created to connect people can often intensify loneliness.
- Fake news, misinformation, and manipulation. False information can spread quickly, manipulate people, deepen political divides, and make it harder to tell what’s true.
On a personal note, my wife and I have become much more cautious about social media. That brings us to the third point.
- Loss of privacy. Our personal information has become valuable to companies. Social media platforms compete for our attention, which can lead to endless scrolling, more distractions, and less time spent with people in person.
Three positives:
- Global connection. People can maintain relationships worldwide, reconnect with old friends, discover communities of shared interests, and communicate instantly, no matter the distance.
- Individuals can share ideas, teach skills, build businesses, and reach enormous audiences without traditional publishers, broadcasters, or other gatekeepers.
- Social awareness and collective action. Social media can expose injustice, organize relief efforts, amplify overlooked voices, and activate communities during emergencies.
After weeks of work, I’ve created a link to artificial intelligence with my new project, ASK JAMES MAPES, which is like a “mini me.” ask.jamesmapes.com
The ASK JAMES MAPES project is a personal example of how AI can help. Instead of just giving out information, it expands your knowledge about imagination, fear, change, human potential, and Quantum Leap Thinking™. It also encourages people to think about their own ideas.
The combustion engine expanded our physical reach.
Social media expanded our social reach.
Artificial intelligence is expanding our intellectual reach.
But each breakthrough comes with a paradox. The same technology that gives us power can also weaken us if we stop taking responsibility for how we use it.
It’s important to distinguish between letting technology think for us and using it to help us think more deeply.
Think about this question:
“Will artificial intelligence become a substitute for human thinking—or the greatest catalyst for human imagination we have ever created?”
My goal is to use AI to help others grow in their lives.
—
iStock image
articles.summary:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and other observers highlight that while generative artificial intelligence offers unprecedented intellectual expansion, it also presents significant risks requiring proactive human responsibility and oversight.

### Key Points
- Historical technological breakthroughs like the internal combustion engine and social media demonstrate a recurring paradox of providing societal benefits alongside unintended negative consequences.
- The internal combustion engine increased global mobility and economic growth but introduced environmental pollution, fossil fuel dependence, and high rates of traffic-related fatalities.
- Social media platforms enabled global connectivity and democratic information sharing while simultaneously contributing to mental health issues, misinformation, and the erosion of personal privacy.
- The "ASK JAMES MAPES" project serves as a practical example of using AI to augment human imagination and knowledge regarding personal development and critical thinking.
- The long-term impact of artificial intelligence depends on whether users employ the technology as a tool for deeper cognition or as a substitute for independent thought.

### Why it Matters
The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into daily life forces a critical evaluation of how humanity balances technological convenience with cognitive autonomy. Understanding these historical patterns helps society mitigate potential risks while leveraging AI as a catalyst for human creativity and intellectual growth.

articles.title: GitHub CLI's New Expiring Tokens Still Leave Your Refresh Token Exposed to Malware
articles.author: Shunsuke Suzuki
articles.content:
GitHub CLI (gh) recently added short-lived access tokens that are refreshed automatically. It is a public preview and opt-in for now, but it is planned to become the default.
This is a welcome change: a leaked access token now stops working within eight hours. But the refresh token is a different story. It lives for months, and gh stores it in the OS keyring, where on macOS any process running as you can read it without a confirmation dialog, as gh's own documentation acknowledges. If malware steals the refresh token, it can keep minting new access tokens off your machine.
I develop ghtkn, a CLI that creates short-lived GitHub App user access tokens for local development, and it was designed with exactly this threat in mind. This article compares ghtkn with gh's new short-lived tokens and explains what ghtkn protects against that gh doesn't.
Like gh, ghtkn issues access tokens that expire in eight hours and refreshes them automatically with a refresh token, so you only go through the device flow once per app. The difference is where the tokens live. ghtkn supports refresh tokens only on its agent backend: a local daemon that stores tokens encrypted with a key derived from your passphrase. The agent starts locked, and tokens become available only after you unlock it with your passphrase.
For details, see the documentation:
Here is where ghtkn differs from gh's short-lived tokens.
- The refresh token is hard to steal even if arbitrary code runs on your machine
- You can restrict which organizations and repositories a token can access
- You can use different apps with different permissions for different purposes
- The refresh token is never stored in plain text
- You can lock the agent so that no token can be obtained
- A suspected refresh token leak is detected and reported
- Go CLIs integrate seamlessly through the SDK
Let's look at each of them in detail.
Protecting the refresh token is essential to keeping short-lived tokens meaningful.
First, note that access tokens can be obtained with either tool. gh gives you one with gh auth token, and ghtkn gives you one with ghtkn get, so there is no difference in the fact that an access token can leak if arbitrary code runs on your machine.
However, an access token expires in eight hours, but a refresh token doesn't. According to GitHub's documentation, a refresh token expires only after six months without use, and each refresh issues a new refresh token. So if a refresh token leaks, an attacker can keep refreshing it and mint access tokens off your machine practically forever. That largely defeats the purpose of making access tokens short-lived.
gh stores the refresh token in the OS keyring by default, but if arbitrary code runs on your machine, for example through a supply chain attack, secrets stored in the OS keyring can easily leak. On macOS, gh accesses the Keychain through /usr/bin/security, and once /usr/bin/security is trusted (most people have trusted it), it can read and write secrets without any confirmation dialog. gh's own document about the macOS keyring mentions this as well. Moreover, the name of gh's Keychain item is obvious from the source code, so malware can easily get the refresh token. When I actually tried it, a single security command gave me both the access token and the refresh token without any confirmation dialog.
ghtkn's agent backend, on the other hand, encrypts and stores the refresh token on its own. The encryption key is derived from the user's passphrase, and the passphrase is never saved to disk. The agent also has no API that returns the refresh token; clients can only obtain access tokens. Furthermore, a non-root process running as the same user can't read the agent's memory. macOS restricts reading other processes' memory by default, and on Linux the agent marks its own process non-dumpable (PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0) at startup. So even if arbitrary code runs on your machine, the refresh token doesn't easily leak unless the attacker escalates to root.
gh's token can access every repository the user can access, and there is no way to restrict it. Also, gh is a privileged app, so organizations can't restrict its access with their settings.
ghtkn, on the other hand, uses GitHub App user access tokens, so a token can only access the organizations and repositories the app is installed on. A private app can only be installed on the organization or user that owns it, so even if the access token of your personal GitHub App leaks, it can't access your company's organization. You can also restrict a token to specific repositories by selecting them when you install the app.
gh is a single app, so you can't switch between apps, and it tends to have strong permissions. It requires at least the repo, read:org, and gist scopes, so you can't even make it read-only.
With ghtkn, on the other hand, you can register multiple GitHub Apps and switch between them depending on what you are doing. For example, you can use an app with weak permissions most of the time, and a different app only when you need strong permissions.
In addition, the agent backend automatically removes the access tokens and refresh tokens of apps that have gone unused for a certain period. So if you keep a separate app with strong permissions that you only use occasionally, its tokens are removed naturally while you aren't using it, which reduces the chance of a leak.
gh stores the access token and the refresh token in the OS keyring, but if writing to the OS keyring fails, it stores them in plain text in hosts.yml. It prints only a one-line warning and the login succeeds anyway, so users are unlikely to notice. On headless Linux or in containers without an OS keyring, this is in fact the behavior you are likely to get.
ghtkn, on the other hand, never stores access tokens in plain text unless you explicitly select the text backend. And since refresh tokens are supported only on the agent backend, a refresh token is never stored in plain text.
With gh, any process running as you can obtain a token at any time, for example with gh auth token. gh has no mechanism that lets users make tokens temporarily unobtainable.
ghtkn's agent has the same exposure while it is unlocked: any process running as the same user can obtain access tokens from it. That's why ghtkn lets you lock the agent with ghtkn agent lock.
While the agent is locked, no token can be obtained at all, including access tokens, and you have to enter your passphrase to unlock it before using it again. Locking doesn't need the passphrase, so you can hook it into a screen lock or logout. By keeping the agent locked while you don't need tokens for a while, you shorten the window in which an attacker can obtain them.
A refresh token is replaced with a new one every time it is used (rotation). So if an attacker uses a stolen refresh token first, the legitimate user's next refresh fails. This can be a signal that the refresh token has leaked.
When a refresh fails, gh deletes the credential and only prints the token for <host> has expired; please run 'gh auth login' to re-authenticate. Nothing indicates a possible leak, and since the credential is deleted, nothing is left to investigate. Users will think the token simply expired and log in again without suspecting anything.
ghtkn's agent, on the other hand, returns a warning about a possible leak to the client, which shows it to the user, when a refresh token that should still be valid fails to refresh. This lets users notice the leak and start investigating and responding to it.
ghtkn provides a Go SDK, and various tools such as aqua, pinact, and ghir obtain access tokens seamlessly through it. You don't need to expose access tokens as environment variables, which reduces the paths through which they can leak.
ghtkn supports refresh tokens only on the agent backend, so that refresh tokens don't easily leak even if arbitrary code runs in your development environment. gh has no such architecture with a constantly running daemon, at least for now. Also, because gh is a single privileged app, it would be hard for it to let you switch between apps to restrict permissions and access scope. I look forward to future improvements in gh, but I believe ghtkn will keep its advantages on these points for the time being.
Short-lived tokens becoming officially supported in gh is great news, but they leave the refresh token exposed, and ghtkn still has clear security advantages over them. I will keep developing ghtkn. If you got interested in ghtkn, please give it a try:
The content of this article is also available in ghtkn's documentation. With ghtkn v0.4.2 or later, you can read the documentation with the ghtkn docs command. ghtkn is AI-friendly, so if you have any questions, ask a coding agent such as Claude Code. To let your agent read ghtkn's documentation, install ghtkn's agent skill:
When I installed the skill and asked Claude Code, "GitHub CLI apparently supports short-lived tokens now. Does that make ghtkn unnecessary?", it explained the advantages based on the documentation.
For how ghtkn is made AI-friendly, see the following article:
No comments yet. Be the first to comment.
articles.summary:
GitHub CLI has introduced short-lived access tokens to improve security, but the tool ghtkn offers enhanced protection by securing refresh tokens within an encrypted, passphrase-protected local daemon.

### Key Points
- GitHub CLI (gh) now uses short-lived access tokens that automatically refresh, though refresh tokens remain stored in the OS keyring.
- The ghtkn CLI utilizes a local agent backend that encrypts refresh tokens with a user-defined passphrase, preventing unauthorized access by other processes.
- Unlike the GitHub CLI, ghtkn allows users to restrict token access to specific organizations and repositories using GitHub App user access tokens.
- The ghtkn agent can be manually locked to prevent token generation, and it provides alerts if a refresh token is potentially compromised.
- ghtkn supports switching between multiple GitHub Apps with varying permission levels, reducing the risk associated with overly privileged tokens.

### Why it Matters
While GitHub's move to short-lived tokens reduces the window of opportunity for attackers, storing refresh tokens in the OS keyring leaves them vulnerable to malware. The ghtkn tool provides a more robust security architecture for developers who require granular control over token permissions and protection against unauthorized credential extraction.

articles.title: Bitcoin’s wealthy holders turning to loans and yield as investment habits mature: Xapo CEO
articles.author: Will Canny, AI Boost
articles.content:
Bitcoin’s wealthy holders turning to loans and yield as investment habits mature: Xapo CEO
Borrowing against bitcoin and earning income to build their BTC holdings are becoming priorities for long-term investors, Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca told CoinDesk.
- Xapo customers are using bitcoin as collateral and accumulating BTC through interest on dollar savings, its CEO told CoinDesk.
- Experience from previous market cycles is dividing clients between profit-takers and holders reluctant to sell.
- Traditional banks’ cautious approach leaves an opening for specialist providers, Seamus Rocca said.
Wealthy bitcoin  holders are increasingly treating their cryptocurrency as an asset to borrow against and generate income from, marking a shift from speculation toward private banking, according to Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca.
At the Gibraltar-based bank, customers are seeking cash without selling their bitcoin, putting some of their holdings into income-generating investments, or accumulating more BTC through interest paid on dollar savings, he said.
“Customers are looking for yield and alpha,” Rocca told CoinDesk in an interview, pointing to demand from funds and family offices for accumulation and income products.
The behavior reflects bitcoin’s growing maturity, he said. Five or six years ago, the cryptocurrency was primarily viewed as a trading and speculative asset. Today, more holders want financial services built around their existing wealth.
Xapo grew out of a bitcoin custody business known for its Swiss bunker storage. Its customers include early adopters who have experienced several halvings (the periodic reductions in new bitcoin issuance), and the rallies and downturns surrounding them.
The bank charges an annual membership fee of $1,000, combining dollar banking with access to bitcoin custody, investments and borrowing.
Two camps of bitcoin wealth
Experience has pushed those customers in different directions.
Some of the earliest adopters became more willing to take profits as bitcoin reached record prices, having watched gains disappear in previous downturns, Rocca said. Others, including investors who entered around 2018 and 2019, remain determined to hold and prefer borrowing against their coins when they need liquidity.
For the profit-takers, selling does not necessarily mean abandoning bitcoin. Some keep the proceeds in dollar savings accounts and receive interest in BTC, gradually rebuilding their cryptocurrency holdings while retaining cash.
Rocca said about 45% of Xapo customers use that feature.
Xapo currently advertises a variable base rate of 4.1% on dollar savings, paid in bitcoin, alongside a temporary 4.6% introductory rate for eligible new members. It’s a separate bitcoin credit fund that targets annual returns of up to 4% through lending, exposing investors to credit and counterparty risk.
The common thread is the demand to make existing wealth productive.
“The theme of this cycle is yield, accumulation, income generation,” Rocca said.
Borrowing allows customers to retain exposure to future bitcoin gains, although they also remain exposed to price declines while taking on debt.
Banks see demand, but move slowly
Traditional banks increasingly acknowledge that clients want bitcoin exposure, Rocca said. Their interest in custody and investment products represents a substantial change from the skepticism he encountered when he began working in crypto in 2016.
But building a broader offering takes time.
“Big banks are slow,” he said, describing institutions where new products require committee approvals and employees are reluctant to champion activities perceived as risky.
Political and regulatory uncertainty adds to that caution. Banks that previously feared repercussions from serving crypto businesses need confidence that a more accommodating environment will endure before committing resources, he said.
For now, some institutions are doing enough to meet customer demand through investment products, while stopping short of services that let clients borrow against or directly manage bitcoin wealth.
“Them being slow is a good opportunity for firms like Xapo Bank,” Rocca said.
He also sees benefits in a measured approach, arguing that another failure involving poorly managed crypto businesses could damage confidence in bitcoin itself.
The next wave of institutional buying
Rocca expects bitcoin’s next phase of growth to depend on more institutions making long-term allocations.
He argues that some participation through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) has involved arbitrage strategies, which differ from a corporate treasurer deciding to allocate a portion of the company’s assets to bitcoin.
“People called the institutional cycle too early,” he said.
Reduced geopolitical and regulatory uncertainty could help unlock those allocations, potentially pushing bitcoin to $250,000 over the next two to three years, in his view.
Xapo’s customers are less united about the immediate outlook. Some are buying because they believe the market has bottomed out; others are keeping their savings in dollars because they expect further declines, while earning interest in bitcoin.
For Rocca, that mix still points toward accumulation and demand for banking services that help holders build their positions over several years.

articles.title: Jill Lepore: AI Is Eroding Civil Society
articles.author: Nina Verdelli
articles.content:
They dress like gurus, all alike in black, with similar sneakers and hoodies. They read the same books, many of them science fiction. They speak in a similar language, with a messianic tone. They send messages warning of a coming apocalypse and present themselves as the only ones capable of saving humanity from the potential disasters caused by the AI that they created.
According to Jill Lepore, a Harvard historian and 2026 Pulitzer Prize winner in history for her book We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution, Silicon Valley leaders behave like a religious cult, with artificial intelligence as God and they as its intermediaries. In her latest book, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, published this past August, she argues that today Big Tech controls the United States—and, in turn, the entire planet. They wield their power authoritatively, favoring presidents who best serve their interests, and helping to erode the democratic fabric of nations, one fake news story at a time.
Vanity Fair: In your book, you define the Artificial State as “a future in which humans are ruled, and many replaced, by machines owned by corporations.” How close is that future?
Jill Lepore: The place where people can most easily see what I’m talking about is with what used to be called the public sphere. A liberal democracy depends on a free and open public discussion of the state of the world where people can get reliable information and exchange ideas and deliberate. The Artificial State doesn’t make citizens, it unmakes citizens; it makes trolls.
What this communications infrastructure asks of you is not to participate in civil society; it is to remove yourself from participating in civil society, to remove yourself from social relations, to alienate yourself from your fellow citizens, and instead to engage in the machinery of outrage and condemnation and grievance that is destructive to civil society.
Do you see any reason to be hopeful?
Certainly in the US, there’s democratic pushback. Our municipal and state elections since last spring have been influenced by this debate in a way that I think surprised candidates, campaigns, and elected officials. The public has found that objecting to data centers is a way to say no to the entire apparatus.
What are your predictions for the midterm elections?
The polling seems to indicate Democrats will pick up a lot of seats in Congress, but the polls have been less and less reliable over the last quarter century. I don’t think anybody’s really counting on those predictions. Trump’s power, however, is very much on the decline.
And that’s despite the staunch support of Big Tech, both in terms of funding and political influence across various platforms.
Silicon Valley leaders had always been libertarians. They’re really just supporting whatever political party is going to advance their business interests. During the Clinton and Gore era, they were aligned with the Democrats who were very much committed to the future of the knowledge worker.
The switch that came about in the summer of 2024, when Elon Musk announced that he would be supporting Trump, was a consequence largely, I think, of the Biden administration’s determination to regulate the cryptocurrency industry. That pissed off a lot of Silicon Valley people. The Biden administration also had a commitment to AI safety that annoyed AI companies.
As these companies began to turn their attention and investments toward accelerating the development of AI, the Biden administration was saying, “Well, no, wait, hold on. What’s this going to look like?” That’s what turned Silicon Valley toward Trump.
You discuss in your book how Trump quickly took action to eliminate AI safeguards.
His embrace of AI has really fractured the MAGA movement because MAGA is not pro-AI; it’s just Trump. It’s been one of the more splintering forces.
Between the two forces—the political power of the White House and the technological power of Silicon Valley—which has more influence?
The power of the Silicon Valley elite is not national, it’s global. Yes, Trump’s power as the leader of a superpower is significantly global as well, but I think ultimately Sam Altman is a more powerful figure than Donald Trump at this moment.
Can Leo XIV play a role in curbing the excessive power of AI and its adherents?
The Pope has made it a priority from the very beginning, and he has made it clear that this was going to be an issue of his papacy. I think the statements that he made through his encyclical [Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence] were really important. You can see the degree of that importance in the response of some Silicon Valley figures, with Peter Thiel wondering whether the Pope might be in league with the Antichrist and Marc Andreessen trolling the Pope online.
They speak a cult-like language.
A lot of that world has operated using the tool of mystification in the way the medieval church did. They present themselves as the guardians of Godlike machinery that only they can explain to the world and that they are engaged in a mission that involves the possible salvation of human civilization.
If AI truly poses a threat, how can they expect us to place our hopes in its creators?
From their long-termer point of view, the prospect for the future lives of billions and billions of as-yet-unborn humans involves escaping the earth, founding colonies on other planets. We need artificial intelligence to attain escape velocity from the planet, to build the spaceships, to found the colonies. So, sure, the eight billion of us alive today, it's possible we might all die in the course of building that, but if it’s not built, the infinite billions of the future will never be born.
In your book, you make it quite clear that technological progress began with the ability to count and measure, was reinforced by its ability to make forecasts into the future, and it ended up controlling everything, including thought. What do you think we can now do as citizens to further democracy?
It’s important to find ways to participate in civil society and democratic governance that are not mediated by the machinery of the artificial state.
I think that being deliberate and purposeful about when and where you participate is important. There are a lot of organizations that are springing up that are demanding that elected representatives respond more to people’s preferences in this regard instead of nodding along and saying, “Oh, well, in the US case, AI is really propping up our entire economy.” Congress is unwilling to do anything to stand in its way for that reason, but more than 70% of Americans want Congress to do something.
Originally published by Vanity Fair Italy
articles.summary:
Harvard historian Jill Lepore argues in her new book that Silicon Valley leaders are eroding democratic institutions by wielding artificial intelligence as a tool for global corporate control.

### Key Points
- Jill Lepore’s book, *The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State*, examines how Big Tech corporations increasingly replace human governance with machine-led systems.
- Lepore characterizes Silicon Valley’s influence as cult-like, noting that leaders prioritize business interests and AI acceleration over democratic stability and public safety.
- The author suggests that figures like Sam Altman may currently hold more global influence than political leaders like Donald Trump.
- Silicon Valley’s political alignment shifted toward Trump following the Biden administration’s efforts to regulate cryptocurrency and implement AI safety safeguards.
- Public resistance is emerging through local activism, such as community opposition to the construction of new data centers.

### Why it Matters
This analysis highlights a growing tension between the unchecked power of global technology firms and the preservation of democratic civil society. It suggests that the public must find ways to engage in governance outside of corporate-controlled digital platforms to reclaim influence from the "Artificial State."

articles.title: America, You Can’t Get This Powerhouse Phone. It’s a Shame
articles.author: Katie Collins
articles.content:
If the only two names that pop into your head when you think about the best phones on the market are Apple and Samsung, frankly, you’re thinking too small.
Chinese phone-makers aren’t just making phones that rival those from Apple and Samsung; in some respects, they’re surpassing the iPhones and Galaxys — in batteries and fast charging, and especially when it comes to cameras.
On Wednesday, Oppo launched its latest photography-focused high-end phones, the Find X10 and Find X10 Pro, on the sun-bleached Spanish island of Mallorca. A finca covered in bougainvillea and surrounded by gnarled olive groves and roving wild goats might at first glance seem like an offbeat choice for a Chinese tech giant to stage a global launch event, but the decision is far from random. Spain is Oppo’s biggest European market, and it’s only getting bigger.
More from CNET
It’s a story we’re seeing repeat itself around the world. According to researchers Counterpoint and Omdia, Oppo was the fourth-largest phone-maker globally by shipments in the first half of this year. Already well established in China, the company is now seeing growth across the globe, and in Europe in particular.
It’s an impressive feat given that growing a smartphone business is harder than it’s ever been. It’s no secret that RAMageddon, the ongoing memory shortage, is pushing up phone prices and causing a massive drop in shipments.
Phone-makers might be putting on a brave face as they release new devices to the world, but behind the scenes they’re scrambling to draw up new strategies that will hopefully see them through in both the short and long term.
Growing sales of flagship and premium phones will be key to their survival, said Runar Bjorhovde, principal analyst at market research firm Omdia, during a briefing at the Oppo event. Compared with the budget and midrange segments, the high-end segment is relatively resilient.
You might think that means more exciting (if expensive) phones everywhere – witness the launch of Apple’s folding iPhone Duo, which starts at $1,999 – particularly in wealthy countries such as the US. But that’s not exactly the case.
Bad news for US phone buyers
When it comes to premium phone markets, none is larger or more profitable than the US. And yet Oppo and other Chinese smartphone-makers are steering well clear.
There are several reasons for this. Firstly, they don’t have Apple’s and Samsung’s long-standing carrier relationships that would facilitate their phones being presented as solid options to buyers. Together with the geopolitical roadblocks affecting Chinese tech companies, this makes the US simply too tricky and precarious right now to make that investment worthwhile.
“The barriers to enter make it almost impossible to go in and actually scale there unless you have lots of money to invest,” said Bjorhovde. Instead, the money they do have to invest is being poured into Europe. (Oppo said it will increase its investment in its European business by 30% over the next three years.)
This is bad news for Americans, who simply don’t and won’t be able to benefit from the full array of choices on offer to people in Europe and beyond, including the Find X10 Pro. In CNET’s review of the device, Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon described it as “a powerhouse phone that’s well worthy of its flagship title,” praising its cameras as the best on the market alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Xiaomi’s Leitzphone.
Of these three, only one is on sale in the US, but Europeans can take their pick.
“It definitely feels like US consumers are missing out by not having the latest and greatest smartphones from the leading Chinese manufacturers,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. It’s especially noticeable when it comes to some of the cutting-edge foldable phones from companies like Honor, Oppo and Xiaomi, he added.
Breaking the duopoly
The Apple-Samsung duopoly that dominates the American market also exists in Europe, albeit to a lesser extent. But Elvis Zhou, Oppo’s European CEO, wants to see it broken completely.
“People deserve more exciting options,” he said in a briefing with journalists. When it comes to picking a premium phone, he thinks people should have a choice between three or four brands, rather than just two.
This reflects the more diverse array of successful phone brands in China, he added. In his company’s home country, there are only a few percentage points difference between Huawei, Apple, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi and Honor.
Xiaomi, Honor and Vivo are all now vying with Oppo for a slice of the European pie. One sign of intensifying competition is the shrinking gap between products being launched in China and Europe, which has historically spanned months. Zhou says that’s changing — the Find X10 series launched in China only a month ago.
When it comes to choosing a premium phone, Omdia’s research shows that buyers place more importance on camera quality than do people buying budget and midrange devices, but also “softer” values, including preferred brand, perceived status and aesthetics. Oppo has nailed its camera system, but the same isn’t necessarily true of the latter values.
Zhou isn’t worried, though. Oppo is squarely targeting Gen Z with the Find X10 series (Omdia research shows that people under 35 are most likely to buy premium phones), and he thinks they’re savvy enough to look beyond ads to first-person recommendations and chatbots that will provide specs-based advice to discern which product will offer the best value.
“We want to focus on the young generation because … they know how to make the decision very logically – they will not make the decision only following the brand name,” he said. “Young people really care about the product itself, and they can get all the information they want from AI and from social media. It’s a good opportunity for me.”
The company has already found success using this strategy for the Find X9 series, which saw its share of the premium European market quadruple between 2025 and 2026, according to Omdia.
But while Oppo might have made headway in Europe, it might be difficult to sustain this effort over time, said Wood — especially given that all of its Chinese rivals are adopting a very similar strategy at the very same moment.
Competition might be fierce, but Oppo is ready to play the long game. “We’re very patient,” Zhou said with a wry smile. “We’re not rushing here in Europe.”
Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs were covered by Oppo. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
articles.summary:
Oppo has launched its flagship Find X10 and Find X10 Pro smartphones in Europe, signaling a strategic push to challenge the Apple and Samsung market duopoly globally.

### Key Points
- Oppo unveiled the photography-focused Find X10 and Find X10 Pro during a global launch event held in Mallorca, Spain.
- Market research firms Counterpoint and Omdia rank Oppo as the world's fourth-largest smartphone manufacturer by shipment volume.
- The company plans to increase its investment in the European market by 30% over the next three years to capture premium segment growth.
- Chinese manufacturers like Oppo, Xiaomi, and Honor are currently avoiding the US market due to geopolitical barriers and a lack of established carrier partnerships.
- Data shows that Oppo’s premium market share in Europe quadrupled between 2025 and 2026, driven largely by younger consumers prioritizing hardware specs over brand loyalty.

### Why it Matters
The expansion of Chinese smartphone brands into Europe offers consumers more high-end alternatives to the dominant Apple and Samsung devices. However, US buyers remain excluded from these competitive options, highlighting how geopolitical and logistical barriers continue to restrict global consumer choice in the premium mobile market.

articles.title: Franklin Moves Bitcoin DRIP ETFs Toward Nasdaq With Dividend Reinvestment Plan
articles.author: NewsBTC Editorial Team
articles.content:
Reason to trust
How Our News is Made
Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality
Ad discliamer
