TL;DR: Franklin Templeton has filed exchange registrations for two stock-and-Bitcoin ETFs. Their strategy redirects equity dividends into crypto exposure, with portfolio rules designed to keep Bitcoin a minority allocation.
Franklin Templeton is moving closer to offering investors a way to combine a US stock portfolio with an automatic Bitcoin allocation. The idea uses dividend reinvestment to build crypto exposure, while periodically trimming it back.
An October 22 Form 8-A registers shares of the Franklin US Equity Bitcoin DRIP Index ETF and Franklin US Innovation Bitcoin DRIP Index ETF for Nasdaq. The filing is an exchange-registration step; it does not establish that either fund has begun trading.
For investors, the appeal would be operational simplicity. One fund could handle both the equity portfolio and the rules governing its smaller Bitcoin component, avoiding a separate decision each time a dividend arrives.
Dividends Build Exposure, Rebalancing Cuts It Back
The accompanying prospectus filing proposes an October 27 effective date. It gives the equity version the ticker FBEQ and the innovation version FIBT, with annual management fees of 0.09% and 0.19%, respectively.
The VettaFi indexes started with 95% equities and 5% Bitcoin. Their dividend mechanism reinvests regular and special equity dividends into Bitcoin at the following day’s open after the ex-dividend date.
At quarterly rebalancing, a Bitcoin weighting above 5% is reduced to 4.5%. A separate breach above 20% between reviews triggers a reset to 4.5% at the close of the second following business day. That is a corrective rule, not a guarantee the allocation can never temporarily exceed 20%.
The funds can use Bitcoin-linked investment products and derivatives to reproduce the index exposure. A shareholder would own ETF shares, rather than receive coins in a personal wallet.
Economically, this makes the reinvestment decision part of the product. Dividends are still money belonging to the portfolio. Redirecting them into another asset does not create an extra return by itself, and a lower entry cost for that asset does not guarantee a profitable exit.
A Different Role From A Dedicated Bitcoin Fund
Franklin already offers a more concentrated route through its Bitcoin ETF, EZBC. The issuer describes that product as holding Bitcoin and cash, making its value closely dependent on the coin’s market performance.
The proposed DRIP funds would instead leave most of the investment tied to equities. That means stock selection and the behaviour of the chosen benchmark could matter more to the overall return than a modest move in Bitcoin.
The wrapper also changes the practical meaning of custody. Investors trade fund shares through an exchange; they are not managing the keys or selecting each Bitcoin-related instrument themselves.
The next milestone is the funds becoming effective and opening for trading. Until then, the filings describe a planned allocation strategy, with fees and safeguards to examine, rather than a live track record showing how it performs.
Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.
articles.summary:
Franklin Templeton has filed for two new ETFs that automatically reinvest equity dividends into Bitcoin, providing investors with a hybrid portfolio strategy managed through Nasdaq-listed funds.

### Key Points
- Franklin Templeton filed Form 8-A for the Franklin US Equity Bitcoin DRIP Index ETF (FBEQ) and the Franklin US Innovation Bitcoin DRIP Index ETF (FIBT).
- The funds utilize a 95% equity and 5% Bitcoin starting allocation, with management fees set at 0.09% and 0.19% respectively.
- Dividends are automatically reinvested into Bitcoin, with quarterly rebalancing triggered if the crypto allocation exceeds 5% or breaches a 20% threshold.
- The ETFs are designed to provide exposure through derivatives and Bitcoin-linked products rather than direct ownership of digital coins.
- The filings propose an effective date of October 27, though the funds have not yet begun trading on the Nasdaq exchange.

### Why it Matters
These products simplify crypto-equity investing by automating the reinvestment process, removing the need for investors to manually manage separate asset allocations. This strategy shifts the focus from pure Bitcoin speculation toward a diversified portfolio where stock performance remains the primary driver of returns.

articles.title: ASUS’s ProArt P16 RTX Spark sets a new bar for creator laptops
articles.author: daniel@windowscentral.com (Daniel Rubino) , Daniel Rubino
articles.content:
Windows Central Verdict
The ASUS ProArt P16 combines NVIDIA's powerful RTX Spark platform with up to 128GB of unified memory, outstanding OLED displays, superb thermals, and a remarkably thin 3.9-pound chassis. It's an extraordinary Windows workstation, but most people shouldn't buy one.
- 
Display
- 
Design
- 
Value
- 
Performance
Reasons to buy
- + Remarkably thin and light for its performance
- + Up to 128GB unified memory with RTX graphics
- + Excellent 3K and 4K OLED displays
- + Superb keyboard and haptic touchpad
- + Outstanding thermals and speakers
- + Fantastic port selection
- + Secondary PCIe 5.0 SSD slot
Reasons to avoid
- - Expensive
- - SSD performance trails competitors
- - Battery life falls short of Snapdragon X2 and Apple M5
- - 128GB configuration forces you into the unnecessary 4K display
Why you can trust Windows Central
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
The ASUS ProArt P16 with RTX Spark is one of the best Windows laptops I've ever used. It's also one of the easiest to recommend to the wrong person.
That distinction matters when laptops start at $2,799.99 and go up to nearly $7,000, but I have a good reason for this caveat.
ASUS has designed this new ProArt P16 (H7607) primarily for people who create more than they consume: developers, engineers, AI enthusiasts, 3D artists, video editors, and professionals experimenting with increasingly sophisticated local AI and agentic workflows.
Indeed, NVIDIA's RTX Spark N1X combines a 20-core Grace CPU, 6,144-core Blackwell RTX GPU, native CUDA support, and up to 128GB of unified LPDDR5X memory. ASUS says the latter configuration can even run LLMs with up to 120 billion parameters.
If CUDA, local inference, LLMs, agentic workflows, GPU memory, or ComfyUI mean absolutely nothing to you, there are better laptops for your money.
If those terms interest you, even if you're just starting to learn about them, things get much more interesting, and you'll want to read on.
I've been part of Windows Central since 2007, having reviewed and covered many keyboards, gaming accessories, laptops, and PCs from all sorts of companies from the perspective of a Windows enthusiast and unabashed PC lover. I also run this site and have seen a lot in nearly 20 years here!
ASUS and NVIDIA had no input, nor did it see the contents of this review, prior to publication.
ASUS ProArt P16: Price and specifications
I focused on two configurations for this review. My 3K Nano Black unit packs 64GB RAM and a 1TB SSD for $4,399.99, while the top model jumps to 128GB RAM, 2TB storage, and a 4K OLED for $6,999.99.
ASUS also offers Nano Black and Neo White, although configuration choices are strangely interdependent. Changing color can alter the display and Windows edition, so pay attention when ordering. ASUS currently lists Windows 11 Home and Pro, 3K and 4K OLED options, and memory capacities reaching 128GB.
Interestingly, Best Buy offers a model with 4K OLED, 32GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage in that Nano Black ($3,399). While it's not cheap, it is still one of the more affordable models, and I think it's one of the more intriguing configurations for the general creator category.
But you can go even lower, as Best Buy's $2,799 model still has that 4K OLED, but 512GB of storage (you can add more later) and 24GB of RAM (obviously, RAM is the cost multiplier here in late 2026).
And don't confuse this H7607 model with the existing (and slightly older) AMD-powered ProArt P16 H7606. RTX Spark makes the H7607 a fundamentally different computer.
ASUS ProArt P16: Design and hardware
This may be ASUS's greatest achievement with the ProArt P16.
At just 3.9 pounds, it's remarkably light for a 16-inch workstation, undercutting the 4.5-pound Surface Laptop Ultra, 4.7-pound 16-inch MacBook Pro, and especially HP's surprisingly hefty 4.9-pound OmniBook Ultra 16 RTX Spark.
You absolutely feel the difference.
The ProArt measures just 0.51 to 0.63 inches thick, yet ASUS still squeezes in an enormous 99.9Wh battery.
Build quality is excellent. I'd give Microsoft and HP a very slight advantage for pure premium feel, but ASUS wins enough other categories that I hardly care. For instance, Nano Black's fingerprint-resistant coating also works surprisingly well. As someone who despises smudgy black laptops, I appreciate details like this.
Thermals are even more impressive. Under sustained heavy workloads, my thermal camera recorded around 105°F across the keyboard deck and approximately 120°F near the rear exhaust. That's a few degrees cooler than both the Surface Laptop Ultra and HP OmniBook Ultra 16 RTX Spark in my testing. Fan noise never exceeded 50dB under extreme workloads.
For something this thin, that's outstanding, since I expected sacrifices in both areas, not the opposite.
Connectivity is arguably best-in-class for RTX Spark laptops. It has three USB4 Type-C ports, with two on the left and one on the right, so I can charge from either direction, plus USB-A, HDMI 2.1b, a headphone jack, and a full-size SD card reader. To me, this is the right port configuration for this demographic on an RTX Spark laptop. I wish more companies would split Type-C ports on either side for easier charging, but some still don't.
All these small conveniences add up.
ASUS ProArt P16: Display, keyboard, touchpad, and audio
Both displays are gorgeous 16-inch OLED touchscreens with 100% DCI-P3 coverage, HDR support, and variable refresh rate from 30 to 120Hz. The 3K panel runs at 2880 x 1800 and peaks at 1,100 nits for HDR, while the 4K panel runs at 3840 x 2400, peaks at 1,600 nits for HDR, and adds ASUS's excellent anti-reflection treatment.
It's also worth noting that you get presence detection, an auto-brightness sensor, and adaptive (ambient) color, which are extra bonus display features I like to see at this price point.
Here's my controversial advice: I'd get the 3K display.
Placing both laptops together, I routinely guessed incorrectly when trying to identify them by resolution alone. Pixel peeping exposes the difference, but at normal viewing distances, 3K is plenty for 16 inches.
Unfortunately, ASUS forces the 4K configuration if you want 128GB RAM (unless you go through Best Buy, which has a 32GB model). I wish there were a 3K anti-reflective, 128GB option. That said, as someone who is a stickler for glossy displays, the 3K one is pretty good for glare, considering how much it bothers me.
I've also encountered extremely subtle flickering on my 4K unit. ASUS tells me a fix is coming, but I could also have a bum unit, so I have to have a chat with them about it.
ProArt P16: 3K glossy
PortArt P16: 4K anti-reflective
ASUS deserves enormous credit for its display controls, though. MyASUS (its main control and configuration app) provides profiles, color gamut controls, OLED flicker-free dimming, pixel refresh, burn-in mitigation, and other OLED Care options. You can even directly adjust memory allocation to the integrated GPU, which is particularly relevant on a unified-memory machine.
Overall, I think ASUS has the best out-of-the-box software, at least compared to HP and Microsoft, with the most configuration options for audio, connectivity, display, gestures, and more, not to mention direct driver updates from ASUS, warranty info, etc. I rarely praise OEM apps, but this is the way to do it. 
This is also the part where I lament some pre-installed junkware, except I didn't find any on either laptop. These are relatively clean installs (except for whatever you dislike about Microsoft's inbox apps).
The keyboard is similarly excellent, with springy keys, 1.7mm travel, and a three-stage backlight with automatic sensing.
The enormous haptic touchpad might be even better. Haptic feedback feels superb; it supports Windows Haptic Signals, and ASUS adds gestures for brightness, volume, playback, and ScreenXpert. Those gestures are quirky, but also completely optional.
The four-speaker Dolby Atmos system is outstanding, and among the best I've heard from a Windows laptop. The 2.1MP webcam is less impressive on paper, particularly against HP's 5MP camera, but ASUS's processing produces a surprisingly sharp picture. Microsoft still wins this category with Surface.
There's even support for the optional $129 ASUS Pen 2.0. Using a pen on a traditional clamshell laptop remains awkward, but it's surprisingly handy for signing documents, marking up images, or quickly diagramming something.
ASUS ProArt P16: RTX Spark and performance
Unified memory allows the CPU and GPU to access the same large pool rather than dividing system RAM and dedicated GPU VRAM into much smaller fixed buckets. With up to 128GB available, that changes what can realistically be done locally with large AI models, complex 3D scenes, development workloads, high-resolution video, and anything else that can consume enormous amounts of GPU memory.
Then there's CUDA, NVIDIA's massively established parallel computing platform and ecosystem. For developers and creators, CUDA acceleration is fundamental to everything from AI frameworks and local inference to scientific computing and applications like Blender. Having massive unified memory alongside a CUDA-capable Blackwell RTX GPU is what makes RTX Spark particularly interesting.
I've already been experimenting with Osaurus and Hermes, combining models including Gemma 4 26B A4B, GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3VL-8B, and Raptor 0.6 4B. I'm still learning local AI and agentic computing myself, and I'll be updating this review and writing more about that journey as I figure out what works, what doesn't, and what you can realistically accomplish locally.
Looking across all my benchmarks, however, there's another interesting conclusion: which RTX Spark laptop you buy matters considerably less for raw performance than you might expect.
The ProArt P16, Surface Laptop Ultra, and HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (review forthcoming) trade places depending on the benchmark, but they're generally clustered surprisingly close together. In Geekbench 7, for instance, the ASUS actually posts the best multi-core result of the three, while single-core performance is separated by barely anything. CUDA testing is essentially a three-way tie. The 4K ASUS scored 187,547 against HP's 187,569, a difference so tiny it is meaningless.
That's good evidence of how consistent NVIDIA's N1X platform is between manufacturers.
Graphics benchmarks reveal somewhat more variation. The ProArt P16's 11,840 result in 3DMark Time Spy trails the Surface Laptop Ultra's 12,771 and HP's 13,080 by around 7% and 9%, respectively. Speed Way and Steel Nomad tell roughly the same story, with ASUS usually sitting a few percentage points behind Microsoft and HP.
Yet even that isn't universal. In the heavier Time Spy Extreme test, the ProArt P16 actually beats both of them, scoring 6,006 compared to 5,857 for Surface and 5,492 for HP.
In other words, I wouldn't declare any of these RTX Spark laptops the definitive performance winner. We're talking about variations of the same extraordinarily powerful NVIDIA platform, and the rankings shift depending on the workload.
It's also worth remembering what ASUS has achieved physically. At 3.9 pounds and as little as 0.51 inches thick, the ProArt P16 is substantially lighter than its RTX Spark rivals while still maintaining excellent temperatures and relatively restrained fan noise. Some performance variation could plausibly be the consequence of fitting N1X into a thinner, lighter thermal envelope, but ASUS certainly hasn't compromised performance enough that I'd choose a much heavier laptop based on these benchmark differences alone.
The one performance result I would criticize is the SSD.
Both ASUS configurations are well behind the competition. Sequential reads hover around 7,300 MB/s, compared with 10,389 MB/s on the HP and a massive 14,647 MB/s on the Surface Laptop Ultra. Writes vary considerably between my ASUS configurations, too, from 4,124 MB/s on the 3K model to 6,720 MB/s on the 4K machine. Microsoft reached 12,711 MB/s.
Those ASUS numbers aren't slow in isolation, and Windows still feels exceptionally responsive, but this is a $2,800 to $7,000 workstation. Faster storage should come with the territory. At least ASUS provides a second PCIe 5.0 M.2 slot for expansion, so you can add a seriously fast SSD later.
Left-side ports on ASUS ProArt P16.
Right-side ports on ASUS ProArt P16.
Gaming performance is also surprisingly good. I've played Gears of War: E-Day at maximum settings without issue, while Minecraft Dungeons II looked and played fantastic aside from occasional frustrating stutters. NVIDIA's latest Game Ready Driver appears to have fixed the latter on my machine, which suggests some of RTX Spark's early gaming quirks may improve as drivers mature.
And RTX Spark is legitimately fast here. Time Spy places the ProArt P16 ahead of the RTX 5070-equipped Dell 16 Premium, while Steel Nomad and Speed Way put it comfortably ahead of an RTX 5050 Laptop GPU. A conventional gaming laptop remains the smarter purchase if gaming is your priority, but RTX Spark owners certainly don't need a second computer just to play PC games.
Ultimately, that's the performance story of the ProArt P16: ASUS gives up remarkably little despite building one of the lightest and thinnest RTX Spark laptops I've tested. Its N1X CPU and CUDA performance are right up there with Surface and HP; GPU performance is sometimes a little behind and sometimes ahead, and the only consistent disappointment is the SSD.
For a machine that's almost a full pound lighter than HP's OmniBook Ultra 16, I'll happily make that trade.
ASUS ProArt P16: Battery life
Battery life is good given what's inside (a 99.9 WHr battery, the legal limit), though Apple and Qualcomm still have an obvious efficiency advantage here, and I expect NVIDIA to improve over the coming years.
The Windows Battery Report recorded 9 hours and 58 minutes of real-world usage averaged over several weeks, including web browsing, video, messaging, and lighter creative work, basically standard laptop work with more focus on multimedia production and some lighter local AI work.
Hammer the GPU continuously with rendering, AI, or gaming and expect substantially less. Physics eventually wins.
Still, I can't say I've ever had a Windows laptop this powerful, this capable, and this thin/ligyht, and still get that kind of "regular" battery life.
Standby performance is exceptional. Leaving the ProArt P16 overnight resulted in less than 1% battery loss over 14 hours, finally making this Windows laptop behave the way I expect a modern premium portable PC to.
The included 140W USB-C charger is slightly bigger than HP's, though still compact, and ASUS gets bonus points for the excellent thick braided cable.
ASUS ProArt P16: Should you buy it?
✅You should buy this if ...
- You know the benefits of unified memory and CUDA
- You want the best RTX Spark laptop
- You want to learn about cutting-edge agentic AI workflows
- You need a light, very capable workstation for 3D creation, video editing, or coding
❌You should not buy this if ...
- You think this is just a gaming laptop in disguise
- You don't know what agentic AI is and don't care to learn about it
- You spend most of your time consuming content instead of creating it
So, should you buy the ASUS ProArt P16 with RTX Spark? Probably not.
And I mean that as a compliment.
The ProArt P16 H7607 is a specialized workstation for people operating near the frontier of what portable Windows computers can do. Someone mainly browsing the web, writing documents, editing the occasional photo, or even gaming can get an excellent laptop for dramatically less money.
But developers, creators, 3D professionals, AI researchers, and people seriously experimenting with local models and agentic workflows finally have what Windows has desperately needed: a thin, premium laptop that combines massive unified memory with NVIDIA RTX graphics and CUDA.
That's a really big deal.
ASUS then wraps that technology in what is arguably the best RTX Spark chassis on the market. And I mean that. ASUS has been killing it on design and features over the last 3 years.
At 3.9 pounds, the laptop almost feels impossibly light (for its class). The OLED display is beautiful, the keyboard and haptic touchpad are excellent, the speakers are outstanding, the ports are plentiful, the thermals are exceptional, and ASUS offers a level of hardware customization through MyASUS that competitors should copy.
Even the weird stuff is charming. My $4,399 3K review unit included ASUS's excellent $99 ProArt MD301 mouse and a protective sleeve, while the $6,999 128GB machine inexplicably included neither. ASUS notes that bundled accessories vary by country and territory, so your experience may differ.
One caveat: Those 24GB and 32GB Best Buy models are, I think, perfect, more general laptops for creators who want a premium Windows 11 experience with the latest technology. That's an easy recommendation if you can afford it.
The SSD should be faster, battery life can't match the best Snapdragon X2 or Apple Silicon laptops, and $7,000 is still an extraordinary amount of money for any laptop (though about $150 cheaper than a similarly spec'd MacBook Pro 16).
Yet none of those complaints change my overall impression.
The ASUS ProArt P16 is one of the best laptops I've ever used. For the relatively small group of people who can actually exploit everything RTX Spark offers, it may also be one of the most exciting Windows PCs in years.
And if you're simply curious about local AI and want to learn where personal computing may be heading next, the ProArt P16 deserves a spot very near the top of your shortlist.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Daniel Rubino is the Editor-in-Chief of Windows Central. He is also the head reviewer, podcast co-host, and lead analyst. He has been covering Microsoft since 2007, when this site was called WMExperts (and later Windows Phone Central). His interests include Windows, laptops, next-gen computing, and wearable tech. He has reviewed laptops for over 10 years and is particularly fond of Qualcomm processors, new form factors, and thin-and-light PCs. Before all this tech stuff, he worked on a Ph.D. in linguistics studying brain and syntax, performed polysomnographs in NYC, and was a motion-picture operator for 17 years.

articles.title: Top Stories: Apple 'Pro and Tell' Debut, iPhone Duo Launch, and More
articles.author: MacRumors Staff
articles.content:
Yet another busy week for Apple saw a teaser for even more product announcements coming next week, plus we got the highly anticipated launch of Apple's first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo.
Other news this week included Verizon announcing a hefty monthly charge for the iPhone Handoff feature that lets two iPhones share the same phone number, while the public release of iOS 27.2 and related updates appears to be right around the corner, so read on below for all of the details on these stories and more!
Top Stories
Apple Announcing New Products Next Week: 'Pro and Tell'
The Apple launch parade continues, with Apple teasing another set of product introductions next week under the tagline "Pro and tell." Apple is holding a media "experience" for the new products in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28, so we're expecting a wave of press releases that day.
The event tagline and animated logo are suggestive of the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook that looks like it will be appearing as part of the MacBook Pro family rather than as a separate "MacBook Ultra." We're also expecting an iPad mini 8 with an OLED display, as well as updated iMac and low-end 14-inch MacBook Pro models featuring the M6 chip. Be sure to check out our overview of launch expectations for more details.
iPhone Duo Brings Back Long Lines at Apple Stores
After Apple saw "extraordinary" demand for the iPhone Duo on pre-order launch day last week that quickly saw shipping estimates slip all the way until January 2027, some customers held out hope of being able to score a unit on a walk-in basis at an Apple Store when sales began on Friday.
The situation marked a return to long lines at many Apple retail stores, a phenomenon that had largely disappeared in recent years as Apple emphasized offering online orders with pickup appointments rather than first come, first served walk-in sales.
Some retail store staff were advised to discourage walk-in customers from coming in on Friday with expectations of buying the device, and Apple said it would have "limited" availability of iPhone Duo in its stores in most countries.
A few lucky customers were able to score walk-in purchases of the iPhone Duo, and Apple appears to be reviving online ordering for in-store pickup that was quickly removed under the crush of pre-order day.
Here's What Apple's Apps Look Like on the iPhone Duo
We had been a bit light on details about just what apps would look like on the iPhone Duo's new form factor, but App Store screenshots revealed ahead of the launch how some more of Apple's stock apps have been adapted for the new device.
Early media reviews also gave us a bit better look at the situation, with many noting that third-party apps may not look great until developers get them updated, as by default they continue to show in a traditional iPhone aspect ratio and layout surrounded by black bars.
Verizon Will Charge $10 a Month for iPhone Handoff
With iOS 27, Apple introduced a new feature called iPhone Handoff that lets you quickly swap back-and-forth between two phones with one phone number. The feature seems particularly convenient for the iPhone Duo launch, with some users perhaps wanting to carry different iPhone form factors at different times depending on their needs.
iPhone Handoff does require carrier support, which is still quite limited, and carriers can charge extra for those looking to take advantage of the feature. T-Mobile was the first U.S. carrier to add support for it with pricing set at $5 per month, and Verizon has now announced that it too will be adding iPhone Handoff support but at a heftier $10-per-month price point.
Apple Releases iOS 27.2 Release Candidate
Apple this week seeded the release candidates of iOS 27.2 and related updates for testing purposes, suggesting a full public release could come next week.
The beta period was used to test a revamped Health app, but that has been removed for the public release as Apple will continue testing it before rolling it out to everyone later this year. Other feature additions include a new icon and theme for Apple Music alongside a just-announced rebrand, user profiles in the Apple TV app, and an expansion of Siri AI support to new languages.
Apple Planning 'HomeView Max' With 9-Inch, 360-Degree Screen
Apple's new HomeView smart home hub hasn't made it into customers' hands yet, but we're hearing continued rumors about a more advanced version that could arrive in the next year or two.

articles.title: Battery drain in One UI 9? Some Galaxy S24 users are having a rough time
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Reports from Galaxy S24 users claim their phones are experiencing severe battery drain issues after One UI 9.
- One device under "heavy use" reportedly dropped 95% in a little over five hours; however, it appears quite excessive in nature.
- Another report from a Galaxy S25 user states their device dropped a whopping 40% while sitting idle.
- A recent report from a Korean Galaxy S26 user states their device locked up after downloading One UI 9 due a "webpage unavailable bug."
Samsung has had a busy month. One UI 9 is rolling out on its current-gen and past-gen phones, but it's the latter that's worse off.
A Galaxy S24 Ultra user has reportedly experienced severe battery drain since downloading Samsung's One UI 9 update (via SammyFans). The phone's battery reportedly consumed 95% of its charge in five hours and twenty minutes. The post states this was after "heavy use." However, this might seem a bit excessive. The Galaxy S24 Ultra in question only reported a little over three hours of "screen-on time" (SoT).
It's unclear how widespread the problem is. Some users haven't noticed vastly different battery experiences since downloading One UI 9, while others have. A 9to5Google highlighted a Reddit thread discussing whether or not the Galaxy S24 is suffering from extreme battery drain. Curiously, one user reports horrendous idle battery drain with their phone.
One user had only two and a half hours of SoT, and their battery dropped significantly. In almost 11 hours, their battery lost 40% of its charge while sitting idle. More users continued to share their "since last charge" data. Users with higher SoT showed understandable battery drain.
The folks at 9to5 noticed some reports concerning the Galaxy S25 series. A user said they've had to start charging their phone multiple times a day to get through. We've not noticed any significant changes in our Galaxy S25 Ultra, so this could be one of those weird case-by-case situations.
Bumps in the road
I hate tech problems. I'll always hate tech problems. But nothing's more frustrating than when you're struggling from something, but many others aren't. At that point, where do you find your answers? These battery drain issues have been gaining traction. I've seen reports on Samsung's community forums, and of course, there's Reddit, too. If something is amiss, hopefully Samsung sees it and can help those affected.
The situation only gets weirder when you factor in the strange setup bug that one Korean user encountered with One UI 9. The user states they're unable to get to the lock and home screens after updating to Android 17. They are consistently given an error on the final step, but Samsung responded quickly. To fix the "webpage is unavailable" error, Samsung said to ensure the browser is updated. What's more, it recommends switching to a stable Wi-Fi connection.
This is another that's not widespread. However, Samsung might roll out a fix for this to cover its bases and make sure more users aren't affected. The only question is when that might happen.

articles.title: Researchers Push Over 2 Million Updates to Remotely Disable Popcorn Time Updater That Could Fuel a Botnet
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Between November 2025 and March 2026, the Dutch security firm Eye Security pushed more than 2 million updates to computers it did not own to switch off a background updater that it said could have allowed an outsider to take over the machine.
The updater belongs to Time4Popcorn, an abandoned copy of Popcorn Time, a free app that streamed pirated films and TV over BitTorrent.
Popcorn Time was popular about a decade ago, and the original shut down in 2014, but several copies kept running under the same name. A separate, legal project that took the Popcorn Time name in early 2025 is unrelated to it.
Eye Security, which monitors client networks for threats, found the updater during a routine threat hunt: a program called Updater.exe on one client's laptop kept trying to reach a web address that was no longer registered.
The firm registered the address itself to see what would connect, and about 50 requests a second poured in. It later laid out the operation, which it named Operation IXIM, in a write-up and a talk at Hack.lu on October 22.
Over six months, those requests carried more than 3.8 million different hardware IDs. The IDs proved an unreliable way to count machines, because some Windows PCs shared one and some Macs changed theirs, so Eye revised its estimate to 2.5 to 3 million Windows computers and 250,000 to 350,000 Macs.
The updater ran in the background on Windows and Mac from the moment the computer started. It checked for new versions over an unencrypted connection and installed whatever it was sent, at the highest privilege level, called SYSTEM on Windows and root on Mac, without checking who sent it.
Because the web addresses it called had been abandoned, Eye said, anyone who registered the right one could have served their own program to every machine still calling it.
On a machine with that access, an attacker could install ransomware, steal saved passwords, or pull the computer into a botnet, Eye said. Mapping a sample of the connecting addresses, the firm said it saw home users around the world, as well as machines on government, military, and corporate networks, though it added that it is "hard to draw conclusions" from that.
Eye had disclosed the flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in June. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rates it 9.8 out of 10. It affects three versions of the Time4Popcorn software:
- Windows, up to and including 6.2.1.18
- Mac, up to and including 6.2.1.17
- Android, up to and including 3.5.0.173
Turning the Updater Against Itself
With no company left to fix the software and no patch coming, Eye decided to use the updater against itself. After taking legal advice, it served the machines an update that does one thing: it stops and disables the updater, deleting no files and collecting nothing.
Eye compared the step to Operation Ladybird in 2021, when Dutch police pushed an update to computers infected with the Emotet botnet to disable the malware on them.
The difference, Eye said, is that Emotet's victims never chose to be infected, while Popcorn Time's users installed the app themselves. Still, the firm said, "none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years."
Soon after the updates began, someone uploaded Eye's update to VirusTotal, and antivirus engines started flagging it as malware, a fair description of a program that disables a Windows service. Because every product that blocked it left the vulnerable updater running, Eye reworked the update until only one scanner continued to flag it.
By December 2025, Eye had updated more than 1 million systems and cut the traffic to its web addresses by about 90 percent. By March 1, it was sending about 5,000 updates a day, a 98 percent reduction. Judging the remaining numbers too small to interest a botnet operator, Eye stopped, having sent more than 2 million update downloads in all.
In late March, Eye handed the 15 web addresses it controlled to the Shadowserver Foundation, a non-profit that takes abandoned and malicious domains out of circulation, so a trusted party would hold them rather than Eye.
Public registration records for one of them, popcorntimeupd[.]xyz, now point to Shadowserver's sinkhole servers, with a transfer dated March 20, 2026. Other addresses the updater calls were never Eye's to take and remain with outside owners, the firm said, so machines that reach those are still exposed.
Eye found no sign that anyone else was serving code through the addresses: the ones already registered by other people were parked or up for sale, not pushing updates to the machines calling them. The flaw is not listed in CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 23, 2026.
What Popcorn Time Users Should Do
Switching off the updater does not make the app safe. Eye said Popcorn Time runs on a 2014 browser engine with its security sandbox turned off, loads content over unencrypted connections, and pulls in code from other abandoned web addresses.
Eye registered those abandoned addresses too, which it said would have let it run its own code on every machine that opened the app. It did not, but it built a working proof of concept, so the risk is real. The update only changed the updater, so the rest of the app remains dangerous for anyone who keeps using Popcorn Time.
Eye's advice is to uninstall Popcorn Time. The updater can also be turned off by hand: on Windows with two commands that stop and disable its "Update service," and on a Mac with one that unloads the PT.updd helper. Removing the app is the safer step, because disabling the updater leaves the rest of it in place.
- Windows: sc.exe stop "Update service"
- Windows: sc.exe config "Update service" start= disabled
- Mac: launchctl unload -w /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist
On Android, the updater is built into the app and cannot be turned off on its own, and it installs only if the user taps to accept, so Eye did not send updates to Android devices. Removing the app is the only fix there.
To check a network, defenders can look for the two updater files, Updater.exe on Windows and PT.updd on Mac, and for traffic to the web addresses in Eye's write-up, which lists all 20 domains and the file hashes.
articles.summary:
Dutch security firm Eye Security disabled a dangerous background updater in the abandoned Time4Popcorn app by pushing over 2 million remote updates to vulnerable Windows and Mac computers.

### Key Points
- Eye Security identified a critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in the abandoned Popcorn Time fork known as Time4Popcorn.
- The flaw allowed the software to install unauthorized code at the highest system privilege level via unencrypted connections to expired web domains.
- Between November 2025 and March 2026, Eye Security pushed updates to disable the vulnerable updater on millions of affected devices globally.
- The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) assigned the vulnerability a high severity score of 9.8 out of 10.
- Eye Security transferred control of the hijacked domains to the non-profit Shadowserver Foundation in March 2026 to prevent future exploitation.

### Why it Matters
This operation highlights the significant security risks posed by abandoned software that maintains persistent, high-privilege background processes. While Eye Security successfully mitigated the immediate threat, users remain vulnerable if they continue to run the outdated application, which lacks modern security protections.

articles.title: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology
articles.author: steve blank
articles.content:
I’ve been in London for the last month and have heard policymakers react to the wake up call Elon Musk just delivered.
The decision of the U.S. to shut off intelligence and throttle the military version of Starlink called Starshield to Ukraine may have been a blip in the news in the US, but it has sent tremors across Europe.
For years doomsayers in the UK and Europe were worried about the U.S. having a kill switch in weapon systems and critical commercial technology that could disconnect them at will. Most people, including me, thought that it was a paranoid fantasy.
Until it happened. Seemingly on a whim of a single individual, (according to the Wall Street Journal) Elon Musk personally ordered the restrictions, and the effect was to tilt Russia’s war against Ukraine in favor of the Russians. This wasn’t an articulated U.S. foreign policy nor was it an announced act of the U.S. government. From news accounts it appears to have been a personal decision of an American CEO acting unilaterally.
Blowback
For whatever reason, whether it was to satisfy a request from the White House or some personal animosity to the Ukrainians, from Europe’s perspective, that’s almost beside the point. An American company operating critical military infrastructure was able to degrade the capability of an American partner in the middle of a war. Without warning.
The message heard loud and clear here in Europe was that the U.S. is an unreliable security and technology partner willing to throw any partner under the bus, at any time, for any reason.
The conversations I’ve heard have included, “what happens if other U.S. CEOs – Microsoft, OpenAI or Anthropic, Oracle, Palantir, or Google – decide to restrict/limit or deny access to their products? What capabilities would Europe lose if enterprise software and/or AI across Europe goes dark?” This was a laughable scenario until this week. To a lot of European decision makers, it is no longer outside the realm of possibility.
The lesson that was brought home was that no nation, Europe or elsewhere, can continue to outsource its national sovereignty and security by depending solely on US data systems or intelligence.
Unintended Consequences
Besides the political ramifications, the business ones are going to come home to roost. If every U.S. vendor is now a kill-switch risk, the allied market for that whole ecosystem shrinks. As it sinks into the European countries that the U.S, can simply shut off any technology, over time they will find and build alternatives. In the years ahead, this may cost American companies tens if not hundreds of billions of lost revenue.
Europe has been debating digital sovereignty for years. Up to this year, the idea of cloning the capabilities of the best U.S. products seemed like an insurmountable problem. And some, like low-cost access to space, still are. But today AI collapses the cost of creating sovereign software at exactly the time that geopolitical risk is increasing customers’ willingness to switch. AI makes recreating the features, functions and compatibility of Microsoft Office, Oracle, Salesforce, Palantir, Anduril, et al. within reach. AI puts it well within the capabilities of most nations.
The U.S. spent decades establishing itself as the world’s indispensable technology supplier. A substantial part of that advantage depended on customers believing American technology would remain reliable and available.
Going forward a U.S. founder selling into European defense or government now needs an answer to “who holds the switch” before the first meeting; and European founders just got sovereignty as a sellable feature.
What was done in a fit of pique will cost the U.S. both leadership and jobs.
Filed under: National Security, Teaching |
articles.summary:
European policymakers are reconsidering their reliance on American technology after reports that Elon Musk unilaterally restricted Starlink access for Ukraine, sparking concerns over national sovereignty and security.

### Key Points
- Reports indicate Elon Musk personally ordered restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services, impacting military operations in Ukraine.
- European officials now view U.S. technology providers as potential security risks due to the possibility of unilateral service shutdowns.
- The incident has accelerated European debates regarding digital sovereignty and the need to develop independent alternatives to U.S. software and infrastructure.
- Advances in artificial intelligence are lowering the barriers for European nations to build sovereign software that replicates U.S. enterprise and defense capabilities.
- U.S. technology firms may face significant long-term revenue losses as international clients prioritize security and control over existing vendor relationships.

### Why it Matters
This shift in perception threatens the long-standing dominance of American technology companies in global defense and government markets. If international partners view U.S. vendors as unreliable, it could trigger a massive move toward domestic alternatives, ultimately costing the U.S. economy billions in lost revenue and geopolitical influence.

articles.title: I spent $200 on thrifted 4K Blu-rays instead of digital rentals, and my local Plex library paid for itself in months
articles.author: Jasmine Mannan
articles.content:
Movie night with streaming services can be frustrating. Sometimes the apps don't even have the film you want to watch, and then when they do, you pay $4 to $6 a pop to rent it.
When you actually watch that movie, whether it was on the service or not, it ends up as a compressed, low-bitrate digital file. Most people believe physical media is dead, but secondhand shops, garage sales, and pawn shops are flooded with Blu-rays that people bought once and then dumped for pennies.
Dropping a flat $200 budget entirely on thrifted 4K discs, ripping them with MakeMKV to a local home server, and feeding an uncompressed Plex library felt like a much better deal than paying for streaming services. When you factor in the true cost of recurring digital rentals, loss of ownership, and the abysmal bitrates of streaming services, thrift hunting physical media isn't a dying hobby. It's the ultimate financial and technical hack for building an elite personal streaming empire.
Streaming services just don't deliver
Compression ruins the quality
When you stream movies from services like Netflix, Prime Video, or Apple TV, you get a bit-rate illusion. It might say the video you're watching is in 4K, but in reality, it is a compressed lie compared to the quality of your physical discs.
Commercial streaming platforms compress 4K video to 15Mbps to 25Mbps to save bandwidth and make it accessible to people without superfast internet speeds. As a result, you get crushing macroblocks in dark scenes, muddy gradients, and compressed audio. It just never matches the uncompressed reality you get on physical discs.
A 4K Blu-ray disc boasts bit rates soaring anywhere from 60Mbps to over 100Mbps. Paired with lossless Dolby TrueHD, DTS-HD Master Audio, or Dolby Atmos, it feels and sounds significantly different when you're watching it. Ripping that disc directly into a Plex remux gives you absolute reference-grade quality that streaming services cannot touch.
The secondhand market is a gold mine
You can grab 4K Blu-rays at a major price cut
Thrifted discs essentially destroy digital rentals on cost. You can easily build a Blu-ray library for $150. It might sound far-fetched when you think about a brand-new 4K Blu-ray retailing for about $25 to $30, depending on the movie. But by scouring thrift stores, pawn shops, and clearance bins, you can routinely pick up 4K discs for $5 to $8 apiece.
The secondhand market is absolutely fantastic for this. This lets you source anywhere from 20 to 30 top-tier films for about $200, averaging about $6 per movie (roughly the same as a single modern digital rental that gives you access for 48 hours). When that digital rental vanishes after 48 hours, you lose access and have to rent it again, whereas a thrifted physical disc is a permanent asset.
Ripping that disc into Plex means it's yours forever. If you want to watch or rewatch that movie twice or share it with family members on your Plex server, the per-view cost drops even lower and lower. It pays for itself almost instantly compared to continuous digital rentals.
How to build your own media library
Turn your own physical library into a digital one
If you want to build up your own physical media library, then here's how to get started. First, hunt smart. Target local thrift chains, pawn shops, and Facebook Marketplace lots rather than paying retail collector prices. Sometimes all it takes is a quick glance over a sale bin to find a hidden gem. When you pick up your Blu-ray discs, especially secondhand ones, double-check the condition. Sometimes there are deep scratches, and while 4K Blu-ray discs are remarkably resilient because of their hard-coat polymer layers, they're not always perfect.
After you find the physical discs you want to rip, you'll need an Ultra HD-friendly drive. A range of external Blu-ray drives is available on the market, but make sure you pick one compatible with 4K. Be sure to double-check the specifications. You can flash it with custom firmware to support UHD reading and then hook it up to your home server or desktop. Blu-ray drives can be an expensive upfront purchase, costing around $100, but once you buy one, you can rip as many Blu-rays as you want for the foreseeable future.
To rip the film itself, you can use MakeMKV. You can download this software, and it lets you extract the main movie file as an uncompressed MKV container, preserving the original video track and lossless audio streams without quality loss. When you do, be sure to select only the audio tracks you need instead of all the languages included on the disc. This will help you save space.
And lastly, it's time to feed your Plex library. Drop the files into your structured Plex media directories, let the scanner pull metadata, and enjoy pristine 4K streaming anywhere in your home.
Stop paying for digital rentals
Physical discs are permanent
The digital rental economy relies on making you pay repeatedly for temporary access to compressed files, or paying a subscription for services that constantly remove your favorite movies. Spending $150 on thrifted physical media proves you can build a high-performance local streaming library that outclasses commercial streaming providers while keeping full ownership of your data.
Stop throwing money away on temporary digital rentals. Hit up your local secondhand shops and start building a Plex library that you actually own.
articles.summary:
Building a personal media server using thrifted 4K Blu-rays and software like MakeMKV offers superior video quality and permanent ownership compared to expensive, compressed commercial streaming service rentals.

### Key Points
- Commercial streaming services compress 4K video to 15Mbps–25Mbps, while 4K Blu-ray discs provide higher bitrates ranging from 60Mbps to over 100Mbps.
- Secondhand 4K discs can be sourced from thrift stores, pawn shops, and online marketplaces for $5 to $8, significantly undercutting the cost of digital rentals.
- Users can utilize MakeMKV software to rip uncompressed movie files from physical discs for integration into a personal Plex media server.
- Building a high-quality library requires an Ultra HD-friendly Blu-ray drive, which typically costs around $100 as a one-time hardware investment.
- Physical media provides permanent access to content, avoiding the recurring fees and library rotations associated with subscription-based streaming platforms.

### Why it Matters
This approach allows consumers to bypass the limitations of digital rental models, which often restrict access and provide lower-quality, compressed video files. By investing in physical media and local hosting, users gain long-term ownership of their content while achieving reference-grade audio and visual performance.

articles.title: That Weird 7-Pin S-Video Port on Old Laptops
articles.author: Maya Posch
articles.content:
Even though laptops from around the early 2000s came with just about every conceivable port on them, they still would often feature a somewhat unusual combined video output port. While at its core this was just a 4-pin analog S-video output, the three additional pins on the mini-DIN connector provided some more features. Of course, as [VWestlife] found out during his archaeological research, not every manufacturer used the same pinout here.
The naming for this specific port differs, with the name ‘S-video+’ appearing regularly, yet many descriptions glossing over the additional pins and only mentioning that it can be used with a 4-pin S-video connector. As it turns out, most manufacturers used roughly the same pinout, matching the shown Dell one. This adds composite output, along with two S/PDIF digital audio pins that could be routed out with an adapter into their full-sized ports.
Of course, the Apple PowerBook G4 had to be that exception again, with it omitting the audio pins and putting the composite signal on pin 5. This left the last two pins completely unused, but serving to completely confuse anyone who thought that they could get more out of the port with an adapter for those uncouth PC systems.
As to the remark at the end about how the transition to ‘just USB ports’ has made everything better, we’d challenge the average person to look at a random USB-C port and tell based on its appearance which standards it actually supports.
articles.summary:
Early 2000s laptops frequently featured a proprietary 7-pin S-video port that offered composite video and digital audio capabilities, though manufacturers often implemented inconsistent pinout standards across different hardware models.

### Key Points
- The 7-pin mini-DIN connector, often labeled S-video+, provided composite video and S/PDIF digital audio alongside standard 4-pin S-video signals.
- Most manufacturers, including Dell, utilized a consistent pinout configuration to allow for expanded connectivity via specialized adapters.
- Apple’s PowerBook G4 deviated from the industry standard by omitting audio pins and reassigning the composite signal to pin 5.
- The lack of universal pinout standards during this era created significant compatibility challenges for users attempting to utilize the port's full functionality.

### Why it Matters
This historical hardware inconsistency highlights the ongoing industry struggle to balance port versatility with standardized user expectations. While modern USB-C ports have replaced these legacy connectors, they introduce similar confusion regarding which data and power standards are supported by a specific physical interface.

articles.title: AI Billionaires Are Flooding Money Into Politics to Influence Elections, But It’s Backfiring
articles.author: Frank Landymore
articles.content:
Unreasonably wealthy AI plutocrats are pouring billions of dollars into US elections.
Elon Musk alone has pumped more than $445 million into Republican campaigns ahead of the midterms, after spending a near-equal sum to get president Donald Trump elected in the last election cycle. Leading The Future, a Super PAC backed by OpenAI and Palantir cofounders and prominent tech venture capitalists including Marc Andreessen, has amassed $140 million to dole out to pro-AI candidates.
But all that money doesn’t seem to be helping the AI industry’s interests, because its image is still in the toilet.
A new analysis from Guardrails Action, an AI accountability advocacy group, found that voters in key battleground states still harbor mostly negative feelings towards the AI industry, with the tech being such a toxic topic that it’s potentially driving voters to cross the aisle.
The survey, reported by Inc, questioned over 3,000 likely voters in Iowa, Michigan, and Ohio — states where close Senate races are unfolding — about their thoughts on AI.
AI, the results showed, is a political landmine, with even a whiff of Big Tech money being potentially disastrous for a candidate’s image.
Three quarters of the likely voters said that they would be less apt to vote for a candidate if they found out they had accepted a donation from an AI Super PAC.
Some felt even more strongly than that. A quarter said they would switch parties to vote for a candidate who took a strong stance against AI companies and data center construction.
“We found that the AI Super PACs were more toxic with voters than Wall Street, cryptocurrency or AIPAC,” Charles Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that combats AI spending that the advocacy group is part of, told Inc. “The influence of AI money on elections and politics sits at this nexus of the anxieties that people are feeling about AI, and this increased disgust people have around corruption and special interest money and politics.”
Ironically, this seems to be because voters are convinced by some of the noise coming out of the industry itself. Many luminaries in the industry have pushed doomy narratives about their tech destroying civilization, wiping out jobs, and possibly being conscious — while companies including Anthropic and OpenAI warn about their AIs going on rogue hacking sprees.
More on AI: An Overwhelming Percent of Americans Now Want to Pause AI and Tax Billionaires
articles.summary:
Prominent tech figures and AI-focused Super PACs are investing hundreds of millions into U.S. elections, yet new polling suggests this financial involvement is alienating voters in battleground states.

### Key Points
- Elon Musk has contributed over $445 million to Republican campaigns, while the tech-backed Super PAC Leading The Future has raised $140 million for pro-AI candidates.
- A Guardrails Action survey of 3,000 voters in Iowa, Michigan, and Ohio found that AI industry funding is viewed as more toxic than cryptocurrency or Wall Street donations.
- Approximately 75% of surveyed voters stated they are less likely to support candidates who accept money from AI-focused political action committees.
- One-quarter of respondents indicated they would switch political parties to support candidates who oppose AI companies and the construction of new data centers.
- Public skepticism is fueled by industry leaders who frequently warn that artificial intelligence could threaten jobs, national security, or human civilization.

### Why it Matters
The disconnect between massive industry spending and negative voter sentiment suggests that AI-linked campaign contributions may be a political liability rather than an asset. This trend highlights a growing public distrust that could force candidates to distance themselves from Big Tech to remain competitive in key electoral races.
